messages.subject: Re: scan1snps summary stats
messages.body_plain:
scan1snps() just gives LOD scores.

You can get estimated coefficients for the SNPs using scan1coef(), but it requires a number of steps:

 - query SNP database for SNPs of interest
 - use calc_sdp() if the "strain distribution patterns (SDPs)" aren't in the snpinfo table.
 - use index_snps() to index the SNPs relative to the locations that genotype probabilities were calculated
 - use genoprob_to_snpprob() to get SNP probabilities
 - use those in scan1coef().

karl

Hi Karl,

We re-checked anything in our script, it turns out to be a bug in our code. Now the QTL effects seems normal.

One more quick question, is there an easy way to plot effect and se together in the same map using plot_coef? Or I need to extract the data from effect and SE separately, and probably customized it.

Thanks

Li Zhang, Ph.D

Postdoctoral Fellow

From: Karl Broman

Sent: Friday, March 29, 2019 10:30 AM
To: R/qtl2 discussion
Subject: RE: [Rqtl2-disc] 4way mapping

The problems with unstable coefficient estimates will not be easily solved and likely has no general solution. Except with very large populations, there are likely to be regions of some chromosomes that give crazy coefficient estimates.

I’d recommend maybe just focusing on estimates at particular QTL positions, with plot_pxg() or fit1().

karl

The "do" cross type is not appropriate, but there's a cross type "dof1" that should work. The founder genotypes would include 9 founders: the 8 CC founders plus the other parent, so for your data the B6 strain would be repeated.

karl

messages.subject_clean: cross_info matrix file for Collaborative Cross (CC) or risib8
messages.body_plain:
Hi Chenhan,

I guess what you are looking for are the funnel codes of the CC which are in Table S2 from Srivastava et al. PMID:28592495
Note that there are missing funnel codes for strains which genealogy is not know.
For these ones, look at the discussion below with Karl :

For 8-way RIL by sibling mating ("risib8"), it matters which are in the 4th, 7th, and 8th slots, because they won't show up on the X chromosome, but also what is in the 3rd slot, because that should be represented with probability 1/3, vs 1/6 each for 1st, 2nd, 5th, and 6th.

It would be nice to work this out once and for all, for the CC lines. It also be nice to have genotype probabilities pre-calculated for the CC lines, so that others may make use of them.

karl

messages.body_plain:
Hello,

In the online genotype diagnostics guide for DO mice (https://kbroman.org/qtl2/assets/vignettes/do_diagnostics.html), one thing that gets re-evaluated is whether the founder majority/minority allele designations are correct. The function you've provided corrects these designations, but only in the context of the diagnostics routine; the original assignments persist in the data one would use to run a QTL analysis.

So, do the same re-assignments need to be applied to the founder and DO sample allele designations prior to QTL analysis? If so, is the function you provide on your diagnostics page already embedded in one of the QTL functions, or does this need to be done 'by hand'?

Thanks very much.

David

messages.subject: CC data in R/qtl2 format
messages.body_plain:
I've added some mouse Collaborative Cross genotype data in R/qtl2 format, at https://github.com/rqtl/qtl2data.
The data are taken from the supplemental data for Srivastava et al. (2017) Genetics 206:537-556, https://doi.org/10.1534/genetics.116.198838

There are still some problems. For example, CC037 is indicated in the Srivastava et al. (2017) supplemental data to have Y chromosome from the founder strain NOD, and to also have a large portion of the X chromosome from NOD. But the way R/qtl2 handles 8-way RIL, this should not happen.

karl

messages.subject: Efficient way to break up permutation test
messages.subject_clean: Efficient way to break up permutation test
messages.body_plain:
With DO animals, n > 1000, 20 phenotypes, and especially, separate permutations for autosomes and X chromosome (permXsp=T), estimating empirical thresholds takes a very long time. I'm farming out the permutations to a computing cluster with many cores, but that cluster has per-job time restrictions.

So, I'm going to break the job up into parts and concatenate the permutation results after the fact. I'd like to know if scan1perms is written such that it will make a difference in processing time if I break up the job by (a) permuting each phenotype separately, or (b) permuting all phenotypes together, but with a relatively small number of permutation per job. E.g., with option (b) there would be some (perhaps minimal) speed-up if the same permutation of the data were applied to all 20 phenotypes.

A third option would be to split the job into autosomes (for which permutations maxLODs are estimated relatively quickly) and the X-chromosome (much slower).

Thanks.

messages.body_plain:
If you’re using an additive allele model (that is, with allele dosages rather than genotypes), the X chromosome and autosomes in the DO will both have 7 degrees of freedom, and so you shouldn’t need to use separate thresholds for the autosomes and the X chromosome. (If you use permXsp=TRUE, do you get pretty similar thresholds for both?) Getting X-chr-specific thresholds should take about twice as long. The time to get a bunch more replicates on the X chromosome should be able the same as the time devoted to the autosomes.

Regarding splitting up, it may be somewhat faster to work with one phenotype at a time, but I don’t think it will make much difference; with a linear mixed model we do the analysis with one phenotype at a time anyway. If you do the multiple phenotypes together and split the permutations into groups, the results will maintain the correlations among phenotypes, which can be useful for some purposes (such as to adjust for the consideration of multiple phenotypes.

In summary I don’t think it will matter and you should just focus on what’s most convenient code-wise. For me, that’d be to split the total permutations into smaller batches, one batch per computer.

karl

On 4/28/19 8:12 PM, David Katz wrote:
> Quick follow-up: I'm confused by the dimensions of $X output from scan1. One permutation for p traits results in a 19 x p matrix of maximum LOD scores. 19 autosomes?

With perm_Xsp=TRUE, the output of scan1perm() will be a list with two components named "A" and "X".
Each should be a matrix with rows being permutation replicates and columns being phenotypes.
The values in the A matrix are the maximum LOD score across all autosomes for that trait in that replicate. The values for the X matrix are the maximum LOD score across the X chromosome for that trait in that replicate.

The separate maxima for the 19 autosomes wouldn't be retained anywhere.

karl

length of the X chromosome, we use n x L_A / L_X permutations for the X
chromosome.
